summary: ASTRAIA: LAST HORIZON is a browser game that teaches space mission design by letting a design succeed or fail. The player picks a destination (Moon or Mars), a launch vehicle, a propellant and a set of instruments, and the game computes from real NASA figures whether mass, delta-v and budget close, then shows what broke when they do not. It helps students, STEM clubs and teachers learn the mass and delta-v trade-off without a lab, with a Bangla and English interface planned. A closure engine applies the rocket equation to a sourced data file, and every number on screen links to its dataset, source, retrieval date and status.
details:
WHAT IT IS

ASTRAIA: LAST HORIZON is a browser game for Challenge 13, Space Mission Design Game. The player is a young mission engineer who picks a destination (Moon or Mars), a launch vehicle, a propellant and a set of instruments. The game computes, from real NASA figures, whether the design closes: whether mass, delta-v and budget all work together. When a design fails, the game shows what broke and proposes the fix.

THE PROBLEM

Every kilogram added to a spacecraft needs extra propellant to move it, and that propellant is itself mass that must be lifted. This loop, set by the rocket equation, is why one added instrument can make a mission impossible. A textbook states it in a sentence, but a learner never sees the cliff. The problem has three layers: it is invisible (students rarely change one choice and watch mass, delta-v and cost react together), unverifiable (many space games use invented or unsourced values, so a learner cannot tell a NASA figure from a guess) and out of reach (interactive engineering tools are mostly English-only and need a stable connection).

HOW IT ANSWERS THE CHALLENGE

Challenge 13 asks for a game where every choice costs something real. Here the cost is real: launcher capacities and instrument masses come from NASA pages. A design closes when the wet mass fits the launcher and the delta-v meets the target, using the rocket equation: delta-v = Isp x g0 x ln(m0/mf). In our two-click demo a design closes with a +0.04% delta-v margin. Add one instrument (MOXIE, 17.1 kg) and the delta-v dial swings below zero. Remove it and the design closes again.

HOW IT WORKS

Data, maths and screen are kept apart. All values live in one sourced file, the closure engine applies the rocket equation, launcher capacity and cost against budget, and the page only shows what the engine returns. No AI model computes any number at run time. Nine automated tests check the maths against a hand calculation, determinism, the launcher limit, cost and the two-click demo. Built with Next.js, React Three Fiber, Tailwind CSS and TypeScript.

WHAT THE PLAYER DOES

Choose a destination, launcher, propellant and instruments. Read the closure panel: a hologram labels the mass of every part, two analog dials show mass and delta-v margin, and a budget line shows cost. Predict whether the design will close before the dials move. Break it on purpose and watch the verdict change from CLOSED to NOT CLOSED. The game then names the lightest instrument to remove, or the next launcher that closes the design.

WHAT MAKES IT DIFFERENT

Every number has a receipt. Click any number to see its dataset, source link, retrieval date and status: REAL (a NASA page states it), DERIVED (computed from NASA values), TEXTBOOK, UNVERIFIED or SIM (game-balance value). We are open about limits: when two NASA figures disagree (the JPL press kit gives 59 kg for seven Perseverance instruments, the per-instrument pages sum to about 52 kg) the report shows both. Failure teaches: a failed design shows one label naming the shortfall in m/s, then the fix. Players can also rebuild a Perseverance-class mission and compare it with published figures.

NASA DATA

Launcher capacities to LEO (NASA Launch Services Program fact sheet; Falcon Heavy is marked UNVERIFIED because the orbit is not named), Perseverance instrument masses (NASA science instruments pages), and rover mass, launch stack and MMRTG power (JPL Mars 2020 quick facts). Delta-v and specific-impulse values are textbook figures awaiting a NASA citation, and costs are game-balance values. All are labelled in the game.

WHO IT HELPS

Students, STEM clubs and teachers who want to teach mission design without a lab or a budget. It is open source (Apache-2.0) and static, so any school or club can copy it. Teacher mode lets a class attempt the same challenge. We keep the impact claim narrow: after 20 minutes a student should understand that mass, delta-v and cost trade against each other and name the source of the numbers. We measure it with a before-and-after quiz and time to first closing design.

STATUS AND NEXT STEPS

Built: the closure engine (nine passing tests) and the sourced data file. In progress: the closure page and receipts drawer. Planned: predict-then-reveal, Bangla and English interface, offline mode, failure replay and mission report. Next: replace textbook values with NASA citations, add ESA, ISRO and JAXA figures, live data fetch with cache, teacher mode and more real missions.
